title: Fractals and Self-Similarity
description: A glossary of fractal-geometric vocabulary including self-similarity, iterated function systems, classical fractal examples, and their relevance to multi-sheeted tilings and emergent geometry.

fractal.summary: A set whose Hausdorff dimension exceeds its topological dimension, typically exhibiting self-similarity at multiple scales.
fractal.definition:
Informally: a **self-similar set with non-integer dimension** (Mandelbrot's heuristic definition).

Formally: a set whose Hausdorff dimension exceeds its topological dimension. Many examples are constructed via **iterated function systems** or as attractors of dynamical systems.

Key features:
- **Self-similarity** at multiple scales.
- **Non-integer dimension** (typically).
- **Fine structure** at arbitrarily small scales.

self-similarity.summary: The property that a set contains scaled copies of itself, either exactly (via contractions) or statistically (for random or quasiperiodic patterns).
self-similarity.definition:
The property that a set $S$ contains scaled copies of itself:

$$S = \bigcup_i f_i(S)$$

for a family of contractions $f_i$. **Exact** self-similarity can be weakened to **statistical** or **approximate** self-similarity for random fractals or quasiperiodic patterns.

examples.title: Exact self-similarity: Cantor set
examples.body: The Cantor set satisfies $K = f_1(K) \cup f_2(K)$ where $f_1(x) = x/3$ and $f_2(x) = x/3 + 2/3$. It is an exact copy of itself at scale 1/3.

examples.title: Statistical self-similarity: Penrose tilings
examples.body: Penrose and AKN tilings are not strictly self-similar in the IFS sense, but exhibit inflation/deflation symmetries (multiplication by $\phi$) that are statistically self-similar — analogous to fractal scaling but with discrete scaling factors.

formulas.description: Self-similarity equation: the set S is the union of contracted copies of itself under the maps $f_i$.

iterated-function-system.summary: A finite collection of contraction maps on a complete metric space whose unique compact attractor is the associated fractal set.
iterated-function-system.definition:
A **finite collection** $\{f_1, \ldots, f_k\}$ of **contractions** on a complete metric space.

**Hutchinson's theorem** guarantees there exists a **unique non-empty compact set** $K$ (the **attractor**) satisfying:

$$K = \bigcup_i f_i(K)$$

When the contractions are similarities (uniform scaling) with ratios $r_i$ satisfying the **open set condition**, the Hausdorff dimension $d$ of the attractor is determined by:

$$\sum_i r_i^d = 1$$

For $k$ equal contractions of ratio $r$: $d = \log k / \log(1/r)$.

examples.title: Cantor set IFS
examples.body: The Cantor set is the attractor of the IFS $\{f_1, f_2\}$ where $f_1(x) = x/3$ and $f_2(x) = x/3 + 2/3$. Both are contractions with ratio $r = 1/3$, giving dimension $d = \log 2 / \log 3$.

examples.title: Sierpiński gasket IFS
examples.body: The Sierpiński gasket is the attractor of three contractions of ratio $1/2$ applied to the vertices of a triangle, giving dimension $d = \log 3 / \log 2$.

formulas.description: Hutchinson's fixed-point equation: the attractor K is invariant under the IFS.
Moran's equation determining the Hausdorff dimension d of the IFS attractor when the open set condition holds.

variables.r_i: Contraction ratio of the i-th map

formulas.description: Simplified dimension formula for k equal contractions each with ratio r.

contraction-map.summary: A map with Lipschitz constant less than 1 that shrinks distances; guaranteed by Banach's theorem to have a unique fixed point.
contraction-map.definition:
A map $f$ with **Lipschitz constant $< 1$**:

$$d(f(x), f(y)) \leq c \cdot d(x, y), \quad c < 1$$

Contractions shrink distances.

**Banach's fixed-point theorem** guarantees each contraction has a unique fixed point. **Hutchinson's theorem** extends this to IFS: there exists a **unique non-empty compact set** $K$ (the **attractor**) satisfying $K = \bigcup_i f_i(K)$.

examples.title: Scaling map
examples.body: The map $f(x) = x/3$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is a contraction with Lipschitz constant $c = 1/3 < 1$. Its unique fixed point is $x = 0$.

formulas.expression: d(f(x), f(y)) \leq c \cdot d(x, y), \quad c < 1
formulas.description: Lipschitz condition defining a contraction map, where c is the contraction ratio.

cantor-set.summary: The prototypical fractal: an uncountable, measure-zero, totally disconnected subset of [0,1] with Hausdorff dimension log 2 / log 3 ≈ 0.631.
cantor-set.definition:
The **prototypical fractal**. Construction:

1. Start with $[0, 1]$.
2. Remove the open middle third $(1/3, 2/3)$.
3. Repeat on each remaining interval.

The limit is the Cantor set. IFS: $f_1(x) = x/3$, $f_2(x) = x/3 + 2/3$.

Dimension: $d = \log 2 / \log 3 \approx 0.631$.

Properties:
- Uncountable, but measure zero.
- Totally disconnected.
- Self-similar with two copies at scale $1/3$.

examples.title: IFS construction
examples.body: Apply $f_1(x) = x/3$ and $f_2(x) = x/3 + 2/3$ repeatedly to $[0,1]$. After $n$ steps, $2^n$ intervals of length $3^{-n}$ remain. In the limit, the Cantor set has Lebesgue measure $\lim_{n\to\infty}(2/3)^n = 0$ but is uncountable.

formulas.description: Hausdorff dimension of the Cantor set, derived from 2 contractions of ratio 1/3.

sierpinski-gasket.summary: A 2D fractal triangle with dimension log 3 / log 2 ≈ 1.585, canonical example of anomalous diffusion where effective, walk, and spectral dimensions all differ.
sierpinski-gasket.definition:
A 2D fractal. Construction: start with a triangle, remove the middle triangle, repeat on each of the remaining 3 sub-triangles.

Dimension: $d = \log 3 / \log 2 \approx 1.585$.

Famous properties:
- Walk dimension: $d_w = \log 5 / \log 2 \approx 2.322$.
- Spectral dimension: $d_{\text{spec}} = 2 \log 3 / \log 5 \approx 1.365$.
- Anomalous diffusion: sub-diffusive, satisfies Alexander–Orbach exactly.

The Sierpiński gasket is the standard test case for non-integer dimension on graphs and the canonical example where the three dimensions $(d_{\text{eff}}, d_w, d_{\text{spec}})$ all differ.

examples.title: Alexander–Orbach relation verification
examples.body: The Sierpiński gasket satisfies $d_{\text{spec}} = 2 d_{\text{eff}} / d_w$ exactly: $2 \times (\log 3 / \log 2) / (\log 5 / \log 2) = 2 \log 3 / \log 5 \approx 1.365$. This makes it the canonical benchmark for anomalous diffusion.

formulas.description: Effective (Hausdorff) dimension of the Sierpiński gasket.
Walk dimension of the Sierpiński gasket, governing anomalous diffusion.
Spectral dimension of the Sierpiński gasket.

sierpinski-carpet.summary: The 2D square analogue of the Sierpiński gasket, with Hausdorff dimension log 8 / log 3 ≈ 1.893.
sierpinski-carpet.definition:
The 2D **square analogue** of the gasket. Construction: start with a square, divide into $3 \times 3$ subsquares, remove the center, repeat.

Dimension: $d = \log 8 / \log 3 \approx 1.893$.

examples.title: Construction step
examples.body: At each iteration, 8 of the 9 subsquares are retained (the center is removed). After $n$ steps, $8^n$ squares of side $3^{-n}$ remain, giving dimension $\log 8 / \log 3$.

formulas.description: Hausdorff dimension of the Sierpiński carpet.

sierpinski-tetrahedron.summary: The 3D analogue of the Sierpiński gasket with Hausdorff dimension exactly 2, making it a 'fractal surface' embedded in 3-space.
sierpinski-tetrahedron.definition:
The 3D analogue of the gasket: 4 corner tetrahedra at half-scale, with the central octahedron removed.

Dimension: **exactly 2** ($d = \log 4 / \log 2$).

Despite living in 3D and having uncountably many points, the tetrix has dimension 2 — the same as a smooth surface. It is a "fractal surface" in 3-space.

examples.title: Dimension paradox
examples.body: The Sierpiński tetrahedron lives in 3D space but has Hausdorff dimension exactly 2, the same as a smooth surface. This illustrates that fractal dimension captures intrinsic geometric complexity independent of the ambient space.

formulas.description: Hausdorff dimension of the Sierpiński tetrahedron, exactly 2 despite being embedded in 3D.

menger-sponge.summary: The 3D analogue of the Sierpiński carpet, constructed by removing the central cube and 6 face-centers from each 3×3×3 subdivision, with dimension log 20 / log 3 ≈ 2.727.
menger-sponge.definition:
The 3D analogue of the Sierpiński carpet. Divide a cube into $27$ subcubes, remove the **central cube and the 6 face-centers**, retaining 20 subcubes. Repeat.

Dimension: $d = \log 20 / \log 3 \approx 2.727$.

A "fractal volume" between 2 and 3 dimensions.

examples.title: Construction
examples.body: At each step, 20 of 27 subcubes are retained. After $n$ steps, $20^n$ cubes of side $3^{-n}$ remain, giving dimension $\log 20 / \log 3 \approx 2.727$.

formulas.description: Hausdorff dimension of the Menger sponge.

koch-curve.summary: A classic fractal curve of dimension log 4 / log 3 ≈ 1.262, constructed by replacing the middle third of each segment with two sides of an equilateral triangle.
koch-curve.definition:
The classic fractal curve. Construction:

1. Start with a line segment.
2. Replace the middle third with two sides of an equilateral triangle.
3. Repeat on each new segment.

Dimension: $d = \log 4 / \log 3 \approx 1.262$.

A 1D curve (topologically) embedded in 2D with non-integer dimension. Infinite length but bounds finite area in the snowflake variant.

examples.title: Koch snowflake
examples.body: Applying the Koch construction to all three sides of an equilateral triangle produces the Koch snowflake: a closed curve of infinite length enclosing a finite area of $\frac{8}{5}$ times the original triangle's area.

formulas.description: Hausdorff dimension of the Koch curve, from 4 contractions of ratio 1/3.

koch-tetrahedron.summary: A 3D analogue of the Koch curve where each triangular face has a smaller tetrahedron attached at its center recursively, with dimension approximately log 6 / log 3 ≈ 1.631.
koch-tetrahedron.definition:
3D analogue of the Koch curve: a tetrahedral surface where each triangular face has a smaller tetrahedron attached at its center, recursively.

Dimension: $d = \log 6 / \log 3 \approx 1.631$. (Different sources give different variants.)

formulas.description: Hausdorff dimension of the Koch tetrahedron (one common variant).

box-counting-dimension.summary: A dimension defined by the power-law growth of the minimum number of boxes needed to cover a set as box size shrinks; agrees with Hausdorff dimension for well-behaved sets.
box-counting-dimension.definition:
For a set $S \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, let $N(\epsilon)$ be the minimum number of boxes of side $\epsilon$ needed to cover $S$. Then:

$$d_{\text{box}} = \lim_{\epsilon \to 0^+} \frac{\log N(\epsilon)}{\log(1/\epsilon)}$$

Properties:
- Easy to compute numerically.
- Agrees with Hausdorff dimension for "nice" sets.
- Can disagree for highly irregular sets.

For self-similar IFS attractors satisfying the open set condition, all three dimensions — box, Hausdorff, similarity — coincide.

examples.title: Numerical estimation
examples.body: To estimate $d_{\text{box}}$ for a point cloud: cover with grids of decreasing cell size $\epsilon$, count occupied cells $N(\epsilon)$, and fit a line to $\log N(\epsilon)$ vs. $\log(1/\epsilon)$. The slope is the box-counting dimension.

formulas.description: Box-counting dimension: the exponent governing how the cover count N(ε) scales as box size ε shrinks to zero.

variables.N(ε): Minimum number of boxes of side ε needed to cover the set

alexander-orbach-relation.summary: The relation d_spec = 2 d_eff / d_w linking spectral, effective, and walk dimensions; exact on the Sierpiński gasket and used as a cross-check for multi-sheeted tilings.
alexander-orbach-relation.definition:
The Alexander–Orbach relation links the three key dimensions of a fractal or irregular space:

$$d_{\text{spec}} = \frac{2 d_{\text{eff}}}{d_w}$$

This relation is **exact** on the Sierpiński gasket and holds approximately for many disordered systems. It provides a consistency check: independent estimates of any two dimensions can be used to predict the third.

For the multi-sheeted tilings studied in this project, all four computational approaches (box-counting, BFS-ball growth, MSD simulation, KPM/Lanczos) are cross-checked via this relation.

examples.title: Sierpiński gasket verification
examples.body: On the Sierpiński gasket: $d_{\text{eff}} = \log 3 / \log 2$, $d_w = \log 5 / \log 2$, so $d_{\text{spec}} = 2(\log 3 / \log 2)/(\log 5 / \log 2) = 2\log 3 / \log 5 \approx 1.365$. This matches the independently computed spectral dimension exactly.

formulas.description: Alexander–Orbach relation connecting spectral dimension, effective dimension, and walk dimension.
